quizzes.stem: A developer must replace a logging library that appears in forty-five source files, and two target designs would both work. How should the session begin?

options.a: Straight to editing, starting with a few of the files
options.b: Plan mode first, with the approach settled before any edit
options.c: Straight to editing, then a plan once ten files are done
options.d: Plan mode only if the library is security-sensitive

explanation.b: Many files and several valid approaches both argue for planning first.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the table says of a many-file change that "a wrong pattern is repeated everywhere", so the first files would commit the whole codebase.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the documented workflow "separates research from implementation so that the work solves the right problem", which a late plan cannot do.
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Importance is not a signal", and the signals are scope and the number of approaches.

quizzes.stem: A stack trace points at one function that divides by zero when a list is empty. How should the fix be handled?

options.a: In plan mode, with a plan approved before any bug fix
options.b: In plan mode, with the division reviewed as a risky operation
options.c: Directly, then record in a plan why the fix is safe
options.d: Directly, then confirm with a test of that edge case

explanation.d: One file with a clear trace is the guide's example of direct execution.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Plan mode is useful, but also adds overhead", and a small clear fix does not repay it.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "Two signals decide it: the number of files and the number of valid approaches", and risk is neither.
explanation.c: Ruled out because "If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan", and this fix fits in one sentence, so a plan written afterwards is overhead that informs no decision.

quizzes.stem: A conversion routine keeps being read in different ways, and each new version differs from the last. What should the next message contain?

options.a: A longer prose description that states each rule in turn
options.b: A request to write tests from the version it produced last
options.c: Sample inputs, one an edge case, with their exact outputs
options.d: A fresh session that starts from the same description

explanation.c: Exact examples remove the ambiguity that causes inconsistent reading.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the guide's remedy for prose that is read in different ways is "concrete input and output examples".
explanation.b: Ruled out because tests drawn from a misread version encode the misreading, and "A test written from the same misunderstanding as the code verifies nothing".
explanation.d: Ruled out because a fresh start should come "with a prompt that holds what you learned", and the same description holds nothing new.

quizzes.stem: The requirements of a large feature are unclear, and the developer is present at the keyboard. How should the work start?

options.a: Let Claude question them, then record a spec for later
options.b: Write one long prompt that covers every case, then build
options.c: Have Claude pick the likeliest design, then build it
options.d: Ask for the implementation, then repair whatever was misunderstood

explanation.a: The interview surfaces the requirements before any code, and the spec carries them into a clean session.
explanation.b: Ruled out because "do not start with a long prompt that guesses" at what the requirements are.
explanation.c: Ruled out because stating its own assumptions is the fallback when "An unattended run cannot answer questions", and here a person is present to answer.
explanation.d: Ruled out because repair means repeated correction, and "after two failed corrections the context is cluttered with failed approaches".

quizzes.stem: Scenario S2, code generation with Claude Code. A team uses Claude Code for refactoring and tests. A scheduled job starts Claude Code with `-p` and `--permission-mode plan`. What happens when Claude tries to edit a source file?

options.a: It goes ahead, with permission modes skipped
options.b: It is refused, with the restriction still in force
options.c: It goes ahead, with the scheduled run pre-approved
options.d: It is allowed, with plan mode treated as an instruction only

explanation.b: Plan mode keeps its blocks in runs that have no interactive terminal.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Plan mode keeps its blocks wherever Claude Code runs without an interactive terminal".
explanation.c: Ruled out because "Edits stay blocked until you approve the plan", and scheduling a run approves no plan.
explanation.d: Ruled out because the exception is narrow: "in an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions are available the blocks are not enforced", and a `-p` run has no interactive terminal.

quizzes.stem: Scenario S2, code generation with Claude Code. A team uses Claude Code for refactoring and tests. After a refactor, one report lists a broken rounding rule, an invoice total that is wrong because of it, a misspelled column header and an unused import. How should the four be sent?

options.a: All four together in one message
options.b: Four separate messages, one for each problem
options.c: The header and the import together, then the other two together
options.d: The linked pair in one message, then each of the others

explanation.d: Problems that interact travel together and independent ones go one at a time.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "Independent problems, such as a typo in a label and a null date, go one after another".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the rounding rule and the total interact, and "fixing one in isolation can undo the other".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the header and the import are independent, and sent one after another "each gets a clean result and a clean test run".

quizzes.stem: Scenario S2, code generation with Claude Code. A team uses Claude Code for refactoring and tests. Claude has failed to fix the same bug after three corrections in one session. What should the developer do?

options.a: Send a fourth correction that explains the bug in more detail
options.b: Ask Claude to set aside its earlier attempts and try again
options.c: Clear the context and reprompt with what the attempts showed
options.d: Switch the same session to plan mode for the next attempt

explanation.c: After more than two failed corrections the documented fix is to clear the context and write a better first prompt, one that carries the broken checks and the lessons.
explanation.a: Ruled out because "after two failed corrections the context is cluttered with failed approaches", and a fourth correction adds to the clutter.
explanation.b: Ruled out because an instruction does not remove history from the context, and "a clean session with a better prompt does better".
explanation.d: Ruled out because "Corrections accumulate in the context", and a mode switch in the same session keeps them all.
